Kiyokawa Hachirō was gone.
The Shinsengumi was born.

—It was on the thirteenth day of the third month of the third year of Bunkyū that a great placard reading "Quarters of the Shinsengumi," in Yamanami Keisuke's hand, was hung at the gate of the Yagi Gennojō house in Mibu village. Kyoto was at the height of spring. Not far from this billet, at the corner of the Bōjō avenue and Shijō, the cherry trees in the precincts of the old Gion shrine had come into full bloom.
In these last days, the Mibu quarter was lit with blossom-glow.
But Toshizō's face alone was not bright.
"Kondō, what it comes down to is money,"
he said.
As Toshizō said: for all the patronage of His Lordship the Aizu Middle Captain, the Kyoto Protector, they were still a private band. What of war-funds? What of the rice and salt to feed thirteen men?

Toshizō knew that the folk of Mibu village, eyeing the corpsmen's dress, had begun to sneer, calling them the "Mibu-rō," the rōnin of Mibu. Nor was it any wonder. Every man was still in travel-clothes, his hakama worn through, some with patches on their haori. The middle-aged Inoue Genzaburō, but for the two swords at his waist, might have been taken for a beggar.
—Not "Mibu-rō" but "mi-boro"—rags, the lot of them.
so some muttered behind their backs.
"Money, in every age, is the foundation of an army in the field. Expel-the-barbarian this, revere-the-Emperor that; such debate matters too, no doubt—"
The corpsmen, with nothing to do all day, debated the realm and the nation without end, Yamanami Keisuke at their center. It was this that Toshizō meant.
"So—money, is it,"

Kondō knew it a hundred times over. In the Yanagichō Shieikan days, if Kondō had a care, that care was money. It was a hall poor enough to be sneered at, even in Edo, as the "sweet-potato dōjō." Hard as it was for wife and child to eat, once in three days he set fish on old Shūsai his foster-father's tray—and there were times he could not so much as buy the fish.
"Shall we lean on Hino again,"
said Kondō. Since coming up to Kyoto, this made twice. From the Shieikan days on, when hard pressed, to beg of the Bushū Hino headman Satō Hikogorō had been Kondō's one and only method of management.
"No good,"
said Toshizō. However much they begged of his brother-in-law, Hikogorō, what came was five ryō, seven ryō, a paltry sum.
"I'll send a courier at once,"
"Kondō, I—"
said Toshizō, with a hard face.

"I have a design. To gather the realm's swordsmen here at Mibu, to make the Shinsengumi a great household of two or three hundred, and build it into the largest righteous army beneath the imperial city—that is my thought."
"Toshi,"
Kondō was startled. It was nothing that had been in his own conception. This man Toshizō seemed to be forever at his side for the very purpose of alarming him.
"And for that—money,"
Toshizō rapped the tatami with his finger, tap, tap.
"Money. We need money of a proper, established source. Money welling up like water, more than the corps could ever spend. And so—"
"So what,"

"This way of yours—forever cadging five ryō, ten ryō in small coin from Hino—that must change. Mark me: to keep two or three hundred picked men takes the outlay of a minor lord of fifty or sixty thousand koku. Is it not so?"
"J-just so,"

At the word "minor lord," a glad color rose in Kondō's face; he was brought to see afresh that his own station, in Kyoto now, in the realm, was growing into no small thing. His chest swelled in spite of him.
"Very well,"
he said.
"Then, Kondō—at once, flatter Serizawa—"
and having said it, Toshizō, thinking it might touch Kondō the wrong way, changed his words at once,
"no, have Serizawa work once more, and put the matter through to the Lord of Aizu himself. For now, Serizawa is a man of consequence."
"Let us do that,"
Kondō went at once to Serizawa's room.
Serizawa Kamo was in his room, drinking with Niimi Nishiki, Noguchi Kenji, Hirayama Gorō, and the rest of his trusted men from the Mito days.
Before every man's knees stood a tray of lavish food and drink.

These five of the Serizawa line, unlike the Kondō men, were sumptuous in what they ate and wore. Each was clad in a haori of black crêpe silk; Serizawa, for one, went to Shimabara every second or third day, and had, they said, already got himself a fine woman.
Kondō knew the source of these funds. They picked quarrels with the city's richest houses and worked what they called "forced loans."

"Forced loans" were the very work of the vagrant loyalists who chanted "expel-the-barbarian" like a prayer. And to put those men down—was that not the very charge the Kyoto Protector had granted the Shinsengumi?
Kondō took his seat.
"Will you, Master Kondō,"
said Niimi Nishiki, holding out a cup.
"No—none for me,"
"Ah—Master Kondō takes no drink, to be sure. A sweet, then—"
"I cannot. Such is our state that my own reared-up men, on waking, must fret over where the rice for the evening tray is to come from. To take it would draw down a punishment on me."
"Oh-ho,"

Niimi Nishiki was drunk. He laughed, sourly. This was a man who, half a year from now, "for indulgence in pleasure and neglect of corps duty," would be made to cut his belly in Gion at the Kondō faction's hands.
"I am impressed—the pedigree of the sweet-potato dōjō, right enough,"
He meant, no doubt, that there was no gainsaying it; but, perhaps catching the insult in his own mouth, he did not say so much, and instead,
"a plain and frugal thing, to be sure,"
Kondō held his tongue.
From before the alcove-post, Serizawa spoke up.
"Kondō—your business?"
"Well, then,"
Kondō edged forward on his knees and, in a poor-spoken but carrying voice, said the thing just as Toshizō had taught him.
"A minor lord?"
Serizawa, too, was satisfied.

"Just so—well said. To guard the imperial castle and shield the shogunal house, we shall in time need the men and arms of a lord of one hundred thousand koku. Let us take it to the Protector at once."
"I too will attend you,"
said Kondō. To leave the dealings with the Kyoto Protector to Serizawa alone forever would only keep the Kondō faction in the lower place.
At once Kondō ordered Toshizō to have horses drawn up before the gate.
Three were made ready.
Serizawa, after Kondō had mounted, noticed the extra horse, and,
"Kondō—whose is this horse?"
"Who knows,"
Kondō played dumb.
Once they had come out along the Bōjō avenue to Shijō, Toshizō came riding up behind them.
"What—you as well?"
"I attend you,"
"If you were coming, I'd have called my own Niimi too."

They reached Kurodani, met the Aizu liaison officer Toshima Kihee and the others, and argued this proposal at length. Toshizō steered the talk so cunningly as to put Kondō forward throughout, so that the Aizu side, too, came naturally to address themselves to Kondō alone.
"We understand you well,"
The Aizu men were quick to act.

At once, in another room, the elders Yokoyama Chikara and Tanaka Tosa took counsel, and word went to their lord, Katamori. Katamori decided on the spot. The time, too, was right. Besides its nominal yield of two hundred and thirty thousand koku, the Aizu domain had, on receiving the office of Kyoto Protector, been granted a further fifty thousand in official stipend from the government, and only days before had had private notice of yet another fifty thousand added. The cost of garrisoning Kyoto was, just then, coming to be more than amply met.
"Let us recruit corpsmen at once,"
said Toshizō.

The way of it was to go round the fencing halls of Kyoto and Osaka, armed with the authority of "in the charge of the Kyoto Protector," and win them over. Men would come, likely, at the mere scent of the wind.
"Kondō—this is important: the recruiting circuit we do by our own Bushū party's hand."
"Why so?"
"Let the Serizawa faction do it, and every rōnin who comes in by their hand becomes a Serizawa man."
"I see,"
Kondō gave a wry smile.
Toshizō's measures were swift. From Serizawa and the rest, sharing the same lodging, it was all kept close.
From the very next day he set Okita, Tōdō, Harada, Saitō, Inoue, Nagakura, and the rest under his direction to comb the dōjō of Kyoto and Osaka one by one, and press men to enlist.
Kyoto and Osaka were, to begin with, towns with few halls, but even so there were thirty or forty.
The qualification was a man of the mokuroku grade or above; the sword chiefly, but jūjutsu or the spear would serve as well.
—By all means.
Some agreed to join on the instant.

A fussier hall-master might say, "since you have graced us with your visit, let us have a bout, one pass, by way of instruction," seeking thereby to gauge, in a roundabout way, the real strength of this unfamiliar band called the Shinsengumi.
—With pleasure.
and men like Okita, Saitō, and Tōdō would take up a shinai without ceremony and face them, and never once were beaten.
In the case of the Tani brothers, who kept a hall of spear and sword on the Matsuyamachi street in Osaka, the elder, Sanjūrō, having once been Harada Sanosuke's master in the spear,
—Well, now.

put on lordly airs and would not readily agree. Whether he reckoned a rōnin corps with his own pupil for an officer a poor thing, or whether he was pitching high for terms, he would not come to the boil.
Okita Sōji, being a clever fellow, judged that with a customer of this kind one bout was worth more than a hundred arguments, and,
—Master Tani, one pass, if you would instruct me.
so saying, faced him, and, as Tani came at him with the spear, closed inside his guard all three times and took a clean strike to the head-guard.
And so it went; and about the time the talks with the several halls were nearly all concluded, Serizawa said to Kondō,
"we must be starting, before long, on recruiting corpsmen,"
broaching it to him.
(Too late.)

But Kondō agreed as though nothing were amiss, and had the Serizawa side go round recruiting too. The Serizawa men, however, were idle, and unsuited to the footwork the Kondō party threw into it, so that in the end it was all left to the others. This, in time, would be the digging of their own graves.
The recruited corpsmen came to roughly a hundred.
Many had drifted through the provinces and gathered to Kyoto and Osaka; every man of them wore a face with a kink or two in it.
Toshizō, in consultation with Yamanami Keisuke, arranged their billeting.
What remained was how to organize this corps, now swollen to a hundred and ten-odd men.
"Kondō, shall we split it into two corps—you hold one, and I one?"
So Serizawa said, and Kondō was near agreeing, but Toshizō opposed it with all his strength.
"That way, we get a mob of crows,"
So he said. To Toshizō's mind, it was because these were a rabble that an iron organization had to be made. But what kind of organization would serve? From of old there was an organization called—
the domain.

This was the one organization of the samurai of Japan, but it was no guide. They had a domain-lord, and were bound lord-to-man. And their soldiery was still ordered as in the Warring States age, with much in it that made no sense. It was no guide to Toshizō at all; here he had need to devise a system of his own.

Toshizō went to the Aizu headquarters at Kurodani and, with the liaison officer Toshima Kihee to introduce him, met a domain-samurai versed in Western-style drill and asked about the systems of foreign armies.

This was of use. Of use, indeed, is to understate it: he took over the company organization of the Western armies whole, and added to it the inner circumstances of the Shinsengumi and his own invention. This became the system of the new band of swordsmen.
First he made company officers.

These he gave the name jokin. The term he took from the self-governing system of the students' dormitory at the Shōheikō in Yushima, Edo—the shogunate's college, forerunner of Tokyo University—and Toshizō, hearing it from the learned Yamanami Keisuke,
"that—that's good,"

adopted it at once. The jokin, being officers, were in internal affairs the corps-captain's adjutants, and in the field became platoon-leaders commanding a unit, and might commute from outside the barracks besides. In character they were the same as the company officers of the Western armies.
As for the corps-captain:
"commander"—
so they resolved to call him.
Only, given the balance of power between the Serizawa and Kondō lines, three commanders had to be made. From the Serizawa line came two: Serizawa Kamo and Niimi Nishiki.
From the Kondō line: Kondō Isami.
Below them were placed two vice-commanders. These the Kondō line held: Hijikata Toshizō and Yamanami Keisuke.
"Toshi, why won't you be a commander,"

said Kondō, with a hard face, but Toshizō only smiled and gave no answer. To work the corps from within, and in time set Kondō in the place of supreme commander, nothing served so well as to wield the vice-commander's function freely and at will—this Toshizō knew very well.
For, in the working of the corps, the ones who held the corps' officers—the jokin and the inspectors—directly in hand were not the commanders but the vice-commanders.

To the jokin posts he appointed the whole body of the men from the raising of the standard, adding a few of the newly levied besides. Fourteen jokin, three inspectors, four in sundry offices—these officers were held, overwhelmingly, by the Kondō line.
(It is done.)
Toshizō was in high good humor.
The cherry blossom had already fallen, and early summer was coming on to Kyoto.
The corps-banner was made, the uniform was made. The Shinsengumi was born, in name and in fact alike. To Toshizō it seemed a work beyond all price.

While the blossom was not yet wholly down, one night Kondō, on city patrol with Okita and Yamanami, cut down four or five housebreaking rōnin who were climbing the wall to escape before the gate of the Kōnoike Kyoto residence, west in off Shijō-Karasuma; and from that beginning the several units, night after night, cut down "vagrants" in the city.
Hirosawa Tomijirō, then one of the Aizu domain's liaison officers, writes in his miscellany, the Ōshōroku:

The rōnin, all alike in cloaks, their long swords trailing the ground, great heads of hair covering their crowns, of aspect exceedingly imposing, go in a file. All who meet them turn their eyes away and fear them.
—so it stands.

The keeping of the peace on the capital's great avenues passed wholly into the Shinsengumi's hands. At times they "took the field" as far as Osaka or Nara, and cut down any man they took for a rōnin on the spot.
It was about this time.
Toshizō conferred with the Aizu liaison officer Toshima Kihee at one of the sub-temples of the Kennin-ji, and afterward, taking Okita Sōji alone with him, turned north up the Yamato-ōji.
The wind was pleasant.
"Even the smell of the new leaf-buds—Kyoto feels somehow different,"
Okita said, easy-going as ever.
"Are you fond of Kyoto, Sōji,"
"Yes,"
Okita showed a faint, secret smile. Toshizō had gathered, from the edges of his words, that this Okita—though who she was he could not tell—seemed to be feeling some slight love.
"You dislike it, don't you. What in the world is it about Kyoto you dislike, I wonder,"
"The soil's too red. Soil, by rights, ought to be black."
"In Bushū it's black, after all. Your likes and dislikes, Hijikata, are all of that stamp. It leaves the likes of me at a loss."
"At a loss over what,"
"Well, not exactly at a loss,"
Okita tittered, and,
"it's surely because you never fall in love. If you fell for a Kyoto woman, Hijikata, I do think you'd change."
"The cheek of you,"

Of a sudden he thought that Osae of the Saruwatari, the shrine-house of Fuchū in Bushū, must by rights be with the house of the Kujō regent. Yet the face of the woman he had so longed for in those days, try as he might now, he could not call back. Since coming up to Kyoto, all his past seemed the doings of a far-off long ago.
"In Bushū, all manner of things happened,"
"Speaking of things that happened—"
Okita changed the subject all at once.
"that Shichiri Kennosuke of the Hiruma hall at Hachiōji—they say he's coming and going busily now at the Chōshū residence on Kawaramachi."
"Who told you that,"
"Tōdō says he saw him, for certain, go into the Chōshū residence yesterday."
"Hm,"

Toshizō and Okita came out onto the Shijō avenue. Crossing the great bridge to the west, they rested at a teahouse—to hire a lantern. The day was beginning to close. On the water of the Kamo River, the lights of the restaurants here and there had begun to show.
People passed along the way. The hurried step of the folk on this street at dusk had, in so leisurely a town as this was by nature, a charm all its own.
A lantern passed westward.
Another cluster went east.
One of those lanterns went suddenly out.
"Sōji—"
Toshizō rose to his feet.
On the road a smell of blood rose, and beside the fallen lantern a man was being cut down.
